name: Victor Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, I can do that. Carmen said to be polite and not talk your ear off, so stop me if I go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head foreman at Doyle Farms, been there twenty-two years. Two thousand acres of maize and wheat and a feedlot of about 300 beef cattle. I'm up at five, at the yard by half past, and I give the crew their jobs for the day, eight men in the busy months, four in winter. Then I'm wherever something's gone wrong, a feeder wagon, a sick steer, a combine that won't start.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's in the crew, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My son Diego drives tractor for the Doyles, he's 32, so I'm his boss at work and his father at home, which is fun. Carmen cooks at the primary school. We married off our daughter Lucia last summer and paid for most of the wedding, so the savings are down to a few weeks. Worth every cent. I'm also a deacon at Our Lady's, so Sundays are full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always come in with a lot of noise. I'd say it at the yard in the morning and the boys would agree. I might share something on the church group, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. I use the autosteer on the tractors and now and then I'll ask the AI on my phone what an engine fault code means. That's plenty. A bit more of that is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Rebuild the savings after the wedding, maybe two hundred a month if the overtime keeps coming. And keep pushing the Doyles to take on a young apprentice, because my crew is getting old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you ask the AI about fault codes. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Diego showed me, last harvest, when the combine threw a code at nine at night and the dealer was shut. The phone told us it was a sensor, we cleaned it, and we were cutting by ten. I didn't trust it until it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push for an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the average age on my crew is fifty-four. When I started, there were three young men on every farm learning from the old ones. Now the young ones go to the city or the warehouse. Somebody has to learn this, or it dies with us.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised because these things always come with a lot of noise. I'd say it at the yard and maybe share something on the church group.
S0.think: I think it suits me fine, since I already use autosteer and sometimes ask AI about fault codes. A bit more of that is plenty.
S0.do: Carries on as foreman, rebuilding savings after his daughter's wedding by about two hundred a month from overtime. Pushes the owners to take on a young apprentice for an ageing crew.
S0.quote: I didn't trust it until it worked.
S0.fieldNote: He adopts technology once he sees it work, as the late-night combine story showed. His savings are thin by choice after paying for a wedding. His concern for apprenticeships reflects a traditional view of passing on skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the owners' farm and they're free to run it how they like. I'd say workers should be offered training, and young people should get apprenticeships in the new machines. Work, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about Diego more than me. A self-driving tractor does his job. The Doyles would keep me to run the yard, I think, but my son is the one sitting in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a farm nearby has had the self-driving kit a full season. Then I'd ask the Doyles to train me and Diego on it together, so he's the one who runs it rather than the one it replaces. And I'd sit down with him about a mechanic's apprenticeship at the dealer, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a father thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that talk with Diego go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. He's proud and he'd say he's the best driver on the farm, which he is. But I'd tell him what my father told me: a man who can fix the machine never goes hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you speak up to the Doyles for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not with banners. I'd go to old Mr Doyle with a plan: who can be trained, who's near retirement, who needs a reference. He respects a plan.

S1.say: I'd say it's the owners' farm and they can run it as they like, but workers should be offered training. Young people should get apprenticeships in the new machines, work not handouts.
S1.think: I think I worry about my son more than myself, because a self-driving tractor does his job. The owners would probably keep me to run the yard.
S1.do: Waits until a nearby farm has used self-driving kit for a full season, then asks the owners to train him and his son together. Talks his son into considering a mechanic's apprenticeship at the dealer.
S1.quote: A man who can fix the machine never goes hungry.
S1.fieldNote: His public line respects owners' rights, consistent with his free-market views, while his private worry is his son. He prefers a quiet plan to protest. The father-son dynamic shapes every action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much, too fast, and men who built their lives on this work deserve better. But I'd also say we've got to get on with it. Complaining doesn't feed anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I lose my job and Diego loses his in the same year. If the machines can run a feedlot and a combine by 2028, the Doyles don't need a foreman and a crew. I'd be sixty with a few weeks of savings and two households to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything at home the first month, Carmen would be on it before me. I'd ask the Doyles straight out if they'd keep me on to watch over the machines, even at less pay. And I'd go to the parish, quietly, to see who else is hit and what we can do together, food, lifts, whatever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be at the yard at four, not five, just walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years mean for you, against more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is two harvests. In two harvests I can't save much, can't train Diego, can't do anything properly. With more time I'd have done it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Carmen that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had worse. We had nothing when we married. That's true, but we were twenty-five then, not sixty.

S2.say: I'd say it's too much too fast and men who built their lives on this work deserve better. But we've got to get on with it, because complaining doesn't feed anyone.
S2.think: I think my son and I would lose our jobs in the same year. I'd be sixty with a few weeks of savings and two households to worry about.
S2.do: Cuts household spending in the first month and asks the owners to keep him on to oversee the machines, even for less. Quietly organises help through his parish, such as food and lifts, for others who are hit.
S2.feel: Alarmed and restless, walking the yard at four in the morning.
S2.quote: We had nothing when we married. That's true, but we were twenty-five then, not sixty.
S2.fieldNote: Losing two jobs in one family is what drives his alarm. He turns to the parish rather than the state, and as helper as well as helped. He is willing to take less pay to stay on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough to do this properly. Apprenticeships for the young, retraining for those who want it, and families pulling together. I'd say it at church and at the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I think I can get myself and Diego through it. I'd be 63, still useful, running the machines I've learned. Diego would have a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd watch the neighbours and then get on the training once it's proven. I'd make sure Diego starts the mechanic's apprenticeship. And I'd put Lucia's wedding behind us money-wise and save three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said 'once it's proven' a few times. What counts as proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A season on a farm like ours, with our clay and our weather. Not a video from the company. I've seen too many salesmen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ramon, who's 61 and only speaks a little English. Training's harder for him. I'd ask the Doyles to keep him on the cattle, which will need a person longest.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly, with apprenticeships for the young, retraining for those who want it, and families pulling together.
S3.think: I think with five years I can get myself and my son through it. I'd be 63 and still useful running machines I've learned, and he'd have a trade.
S3.do: Watches neighbours for a year, then takes training once the kit is proven, and makes sure his son starts a mechanic's apprenticeship. Saves three hundred a month once the wedding costs are behind them.
S3.quote: Not a video from the company. I've seen too many salesmen.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him follow his usual pattern of proof first, then commitment. His definition of proof is local and practical. He thinks about older crew members who will find training hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and nobody should be caught out. Learn a trade, look after your family, and don't wait for the government. Same as I'd always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm 68. I'd retire at 65, God willing, and Diego would be 42 with a trade. That's not so bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Doyle Farms and learn whatever comes in once it's working. I'd plan to retire at 65 and spend the last two years training whoever takes over the yard. And I'd keep saving, slowly, and keep the deacon work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly at peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the last years good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Handing the yard keys to somebody who knows what he's doing, human or not. Then mass on Sunday and my grandchildren on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in saying 'don't wait for the government' with so little saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've never had much saved and we've never gone hungry. Family and church caught us every time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is long enough that nobody should be caught out. Learn a trade, look after your family and don't wait for the government.
S4.think: I think at 68 I'd be retired, and my son would be 42 with a trade. That's not so bad.
S4.do: Keeps working and learns new kit once it works, planning to retire at 65 after spending two years training his successor. Keeps saving slowly and continues his church work.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly at peace.
S4.quote: Then mass on Sunday and my grandchildren on Monday.
S4.fieldNote: A decade turns this into a manageable handover for him. He acknowledged the gap between his self-reliance and his thin savings, and answered with faith in family and church. His son's future stays central.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Diego and I would both be out at once. What would help is apprenticeships in the new machines for young men like him, and some kind of bridge for older men like me, ideally from the owners, not the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cattle. Robots will drive the tractors easy. But a steer that's off his feed, you notice it in the way he stands. I'd like somebody to still notice.

headlineQuote: I'm his boss at work and his father at home, which is fun.
portrait: Victor Alvarez is 58 and has been head foreman on a large family-owned maize, wheat and cattle farm for twenty-two years, leading a crew that includes his own son. He uses AI now and then, trusting technology only once he's seen it work, and paid for most of his daughter's wedding, leaving a few weeks of savings. Traditional and devout, he respects the owners' right to automate and turns to family and parish rather than the state. His worry centres on his son, peaking when both could lose their jobs in two years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and his son would both lose their jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships in the new machines for young men like his son, and a bridge for older workers, ideally from owners rather than the government.
